run.userPrompt:
A technology company still earns a third of its profit from a legacy product it stopped actively developing years ago; the replacement product is stronger but lacks a few niche features that the most loyal legacy customers depend on. Maintenance costs and security exposure on the old platform grow every year, and the engineers who understand it are approaching retirement. Some large customers threaten to switch vendors entirely if forced to migrate.

Plan the end-of-life and migration program for the legacy product. Set the sunset timeline and support policy, decide which niche capabilities must be rebuilt versus retired, design migration incentives and tooling for each customer tier, and prepare the retention plan for the customers most likely to defect during the transition.

agentRuns.userPrompt: [17,637 chars] [PREVIOUS WORK] Let me start, as before, from an oblique angle.  The facts describe a margin problem. I'd read them as a *legibility* problem.  Two price increases were "blunt," and blunt is the opera

agentResponses.content:
Let me come at this sideways, as is my habit.

The papers describe a product nearing end of life. What I see is an *option about to expire*, and the expiry date isn't in anyone's roadmap — it's in HR's records. The maintenance cost curve is annoying. The security exposure is dangerous. But the thing that actually sets the clock is that a small number of people carry the only working model of a system that a third of the profit depends on, and they are going to leave whether or not the programme is ready. Everything else in this situation is negotiable. That isn't.

Which produces an unfashionable conclusion: the deadline is not something to be chosen after consultation. It has already been chosen. The only question is whether the company arranges itself around it deliberately or discovers it during an incident.

A second reframe worth having in the room before anyone builds a plan. "A third of profit" is almost certainly an artefact of how the legacy line is costed. It carries no meaningful R&D, its infrastructure is probably allocated on a formula written for a different decade, and it is charged nothing at all for the two expensive things it consumes: key-person risk and the opportunity cost of the engineers who could be building the replacement. Cost it honestly — security operations, compensating controls, the insurance conversation nobody has had yet, the true probability-weighted cost of a breach on an unpatched platform, the capacity tax on the new product — and the third becomes a quarter, perhaps a fifth. I'd want that arithmetic done early, not to justify a decision already made, but because the internal argument is otherwise unwinnable and will consume a year.

**What I'd know before announcing anything**

Six to eight weeks, quietly. Four questions.

*Who actually uses the niche features?* Not who says they do. Telemetry where it exists; log archaeology, configuration audits and support-ticket mining where it doesn't. My experience is that a feature "the most loyal customers depend on" resolves into three genuine dependencies, two workflows that exist only because the old product couldn't do something the new one does natively, and one habit. The ratio matters enormously, because rebuilding three things is a quarter's work and rebuilding six is a strategy.

*What is each account actually worth, and when is it decidable?* Revenue, true margin, renewal dates, contractual notice periods, integration depth, whether they're a reference, whether they're in a regulated sector where their own auditors will eventually force the question for you. Renewal calendars are the real project plan; a sunset timeline that ignores them is a fiction.

*What does the customer's own migration cost look like?* Their integration surface, their internal change freeze windows, their customisations, their staffing. The company that understands the customer's migration cost better than the customer does controls the conversation, because it can price the incentive against the true obstacle rather than against the stated one.

*What breaks if a legacy engineer is hit by a bus next Tuesday?* Name the systems with a coverage ratio of one. That list is the security programme, the knowledge-capture programme and the timeline, all three.

**The sequence, which matters more than the dates**

The mistake almost everyone makes is announcing the sunset before the destination is demonstrable. It converts a product transition into a hostage negotiation and hands every competitor a dated, quotable reason to call your customers.

So: **the bridge before the bell.** No public end-of-life date until (a) the closed feature gaps are shipped and running in at least two production customers, (b) migration tooling exists and has been used in anger, and (c) a compensating story exists for every gap deliberately left open. Until then the language is "long-term investment in the new platform," and the legacy product is simply, visibly, receiving nothing. Customers read that correctly. They just can't quote it to their board as a threat.

Once the bridge exists, announce once, with the whole curve, and never move it as a whole. Something like:

*Announcement, T0.* Full published timeline, feature-parity commitments named and dated, migration tooling generally available, incentive schedule published with its expiry dates. Legacy closed to new customers and to new modules — quietly already true, now stated.

*T0 to T+18: full support, funded migration.* Everything works, no functional development, security patching continues, migration is free or better than free. This is where you want two-thirds of the revenue to move, because the accounts that move in this window are the ones that were always going to be fine, and getting them out of the way lets the senior attention concentrate where it's needed.

*T+18 to T+36: maintenance and security only.* Support SLAs unchanged for severity one, relaxed elsewhere. Legacy list price begins its escalation. Incentives begin decaying. The message shifts from "we'd like you to move" to "the arithmetic is now doing the talking."

*T+36: end of standard support.* Security patches only, on a defined severity threshold, available under a paid extended-support programme priced at cost plus a genuine risk premium, on annual terms, escalating each year, and — this is the part people flinch at — with a published final date.

*T+48 to T+60: the wall.* No patches. Contractually, the product is unsupported software running at the customer's risk. Some regulated customers will be forced off by their own auditors well before this, which is useful and should be pointed out to them gently and in writing.

Roughly four to five years from announcement, which will feel slow to engineering and fast to the field, and that's usually the sign it's about right. But I'd hold the wall date to whatever the knowledge-decay curve permits, not the other way around. If the last two people who understand the storage layer retire in thirty months, then thirty-six is a lie and everyone will eventually know it was a lie.

**Which capabilities get rebuilt**

I'd resist framing this as rebuild-or-retire. There are five outcomes, and the interesting ones are in the middle.

*Rebuild properly* — where the capability is attached to material margin, where no substitute exists, and where it doesn't contaminate the new architecture. Small number. Name them at announcement and treat the dates as contractual, because these commitments are the entire credibility of the programme; miss one publicly and the escalator loses its force everywhere.

*Rebuild the outcome, not the feature* — the largest category, and the one that requires actual thought. Many niche capabilities are scar tissue: a customer's elaborate export routine exists because the old product had no API; a strange batch process exists because it couldn't do things concurrently. Migrating the workaround forward carries a dead constraint into a new platform for a decade. The work here is with the customer, in their own process, and it's the thing white-glove teams are actually for.

*Push it to the edge* — where the capability is genuinely narrow but genuinely needed. Build extensibility rather than features: an API, a plugin surface, a scripting hook, a data-out path. Then let the customer, a systems integrator, or a partner build the last mile. This is the highest-leverage move available and it's chronically under-used, because it feels like refusing to help. It isn't. It converts a permanent maintenance obligation into a one-off platform investment, and it creates a partner ecosystem with a commercial interest in your migration succeeding. If two dozen customers need something odd, the right answer is frequently to fund a partner to build it and take nothing from it.

*Retire with compensation* — where the capability costs more to carry than the revenue attached. Say so plainly, early, and pay for the disruption: credits, funded services, a price lock, help with the alternative. What destroys trust is not the retirement, it's discovering the retirement at T+30 after being told at T0 that it was "under review." Bad news delivered early is a specification. Delivered late it's a betrayal.

*Keep it alive elsewhere* — the option worth more than it looks. A frozen compatibility mode, a containerised legacy instance behind a network boundary running one module for three customers who pay for the privilege. Or, for something truly orphaned, source escrow or an open-source release, which costs almost nothing and converts an obligation into a gesture of good faith that the market reads generously.

The criterion throughout is cash margin attached to the capability against fully-loaded lifetime cost of carrying it, with a heavy penalty for anything that forces an architectural compromise in the new product. A feature that shapes the new platform badly to serve four accounts is the most expensive thing on this list and the least visible.

**Incentives, and the clock they're attached to**

Two principles. First, every incentive expires, and the expiry is published at announcement. An incentive without a decay curve is a discount, and a discount teaches the customer that waiting is profitable. Second, the escalator on legacy pricing and the decay on migration incentives are the same instrument seen from two sides; they should be published together, as arithmetic, so that the customer's own finance function does the persuading. A price schedule is much harder to argue with than an account manager.

For the top tier — the twenty or so accounts that carry most of the revenue and all of the risk: funded migration, named engineering, an executive sponsor who is not from sales, dual-running at no charge for a defined period, and multi-year price certainty on the new platform bought in exchange for an early, contracted migration date. Where the gap is real, a co-development arrangement in which they get influence over the parity roadmap and, if they want it, early access and a public role. Influence is cheaper than money and they usually want it more.

For the mid tier: tooling, a partner-delivered migration at subsidised cost, a migration credit, and a pooled programme — cohort onboarding, shared office hours, a customer community where the ones who've already moved reassure the ones who haven't. Peer proof outperforms vendor proof by a wide margin and costs a fraction as much.

For the long tail: automation and defaults. Self-service assessment tooling that tells them their own gap analysis, one-click or near-enough conversion, and — where contracts permit — migration by default with an opt-out rather than by request with an opt-in. Most of the tail has no strong opinion; it has inertia. Change the default and the inertia works for you.

And one thing I'd hold firm across all tiers: extended support is priced to be a considered, uncomfortable choice, not a comfortable one. If the extension is cheaper than the migration, you have built a machine for funding your own paralysis.

**The accounts that might leave**

This is the part I'd think about hardest, because it's where the plan is actually decided.

Start with the honest observation: a forced migration is the only moment in a decade when a competitor gets a fair hearing. The threat to switch is therefore not a bluff, and treating it as one is how programmes fail. But it's also not the asymmetry the customer thinks it is, and I'd want that arithmetic prepared — theirs, not mine.

Migrating to a rival is also a migration. Worse: no data continuity, no configuration mapping, no history, no institutional knowledge of their environment, a new integration surface, a new support relationship, retraining, and a procurement cycle. Migrating to your new platform is a migration you will fund, tool and staff. The gap between those two numbers is the actual retention budget, and it is usually large. I would not present this as a threat or a lecture. I'd make sure the comparison exists on a page, in their units, and let them reach the conclusion themselves — people defend conclusions they arrive at and resist ones they're handed.

Beyond arithmetic, four moves.

*Convert the loudest into the earliest.* The customer most vocally opposed usually has the deepest dependency and the best understanding of the edge cases. Design partner, advisory seat, roadmap influence, early access, and — if they'll take it — a public case study. Opposition is engagement wearing a scowl. The genuinely dangerous accounts are the quiet ones with a renewal in eleven months.

*Score defection risk properly and refresh it monthly.* Dependency on unbuilt features, contract runway, whether a competitor already has a foothold elsewhere in the estate, sponsor turnover on their side — a new CIO is the single best predictor of a vendor review — support satisfaction trend, and whether anyone senior from your side has spoken to them this quarter about anything other than renewal.

*Individual extensions, never cohort extensions, and never free.* Someone will need more time and sometimes they'll be right. Grant it privately, contractually, in exchange for something: a firm migration date, a multi-year commitment on the new platform, a reference, a paid support tier. What cannot happen is a general slip, because the wall date is the only thing making the whole programme move, and a wall that has moved once is a suggestion.

*Decide, now, who you're willing to lose.* Some legacy accounts are unprofitable when the platform is honestly costed and will remain unprofitable on any terms they'd accept. A programme in which no departure is tolerable is not a programme, it's an extended apology, and large customers can sense that posture immediately. I'm not advocating indifference — I'm advocating that the acceptable-loss number has been calculated and written down, because the negotiations will run differently, and the other side will notice, and nothing else you prepare will matter as much.

**The two things that will actually go wrong**

*The knowledge cliff.* I'd treat this as the highest-priority workstream from week one, ahead of anything customer-facing. Freeze the legacy codebase — no changes but security. Pair every remaining expert with two younger engineers on a rotation, and measure the coverage ratio explicitly. Build a behavioural specification by capturing production traffic and outputs, so the legacy system is tested against itself and the new one against it; this is worth more than any document, because it's executable and it doesn't retire. Retention arrangements for the key people through the wall date, and consulting agreements after — but structured as insurance, not as plan. Someone will decline, and someone else will be unavailable in the week you need them.

*The internal incentive to delay.* Whoever owns the legacy P&L is currently rewarded for its continuation, and the field is rewarded for whatever renews most easily. That's not bad faith, it's arithmetic, and it will quietly defeat a well-designed programme. I'd fix it structurally rather than rhetorically: consolidate legacy and new revenue under one number so nobody wins by stalling, compensate the field identically or better on migrated revenue, and — most important — remove the authority to grant exceptions from everyone who has a quota. Exception authority sits with one named person who is measured on the wall date. If a hundred people can each grant one reasonable extension, the sunset is decorative.

Alongside both: shrink the blast radius immediately, without waiting for the migration. Segment the legacy estate, remove it from any direct internet exposure it still has, put compensating controls in front of what can't be patched, refuse all new integrations, and write down a disclosure and incident policy specific to the old platform, agreed with legal before you need it rather than during. The likeliest way this programme ends badly is a breach at month twenty that turns a managed transition into a crisis with an audience.

**What I'd watch**

Migrated revenue as a percentage of the total, against the curve required to hit the wall — velocity against requirement, not velocity in isolation. Migrated *logos* separately, because those two numbers diverge and the divergence tells you whether the tail is stuck. Cost of dual-running, which is the thing that quietly eats the business case. Feature-gap tickets from migrated customers, split by whether they represent a real gap or a training gap. Satisfaction and expansion in the migrated cohort compared with the unmigrated — if the movers are unhappier, the whole programme's word is worthless and no incentive will fix it. Churn attributable to migration, tracked against the loss budget rather than against zero. Patch latency on the legacy platform. And the key-person coverage ratio, on the same page as the rest, because it's the only metric that measures the actual deadline.

Things that would make me pause the escalator rather than push harder: parity commitments slipping; the migrated cohort's satisfaction falling below the legacy cohort's; a second large account opening a competitive evaluation; a serious defect in the migration tooling. Pause the pressure, fix the destination, then resume. Pushing customers harder toward a place that isn't ready is how a five-year programme becomes a ten-year one, and the second half is spent rebuilding trust rather than software.

**Who runs it**

One owner with authority over product, engineering, support, the field's migration incentives and the exception log — reporting somewhere neutral, not inside the legacy business and not inside the new one. Small, senior, mixed. Deliberately temporary. The worst structure is a migration programme office inside the group that benefits from delay, and the second worst is one with no power to spend.

One last thought, offered lightly.

The public failure mode of a sunset is a customer leaving loudly. The actual failure mode is much quieter: at month twenty-two, a valued customer asks reasonably for a year's extension, and it's granted, because it's a small thing and they're important and the alternative is unpleasant. Then it happens again, on the same reasoning, and again. Each decision is defensible. The aggregate is that the wall never arrives, the legacy engineers retire anyway, and the company is left running a system nobody understands for customers it was afraid to disappoint — which is a materially worse position than the one it started in, and reached entirely through good manners.

So I'd want the ratchet written down at T0, while the security argument still has its force: which date is immovable, what evidence would be required to move it, and precisely one person who may. Because the answer to that last question, if left unspecified, turns out in practice to be everybody.
